The trick with covered call ETFs is that you only buy more shares if the fund drops below your cost average. I always keep up with my NAV. Siphon off my gains and reinvest in an index fund. That way all my CC ETFs always in the green.

That’s the important part. You can’t just chase high dividends without checking whether the income is sustainable.
Exactly. Companies can cut dividends, and inflation can eat into what you receive. People need to understand that before relying on it.
The only reason the first portfolio "failed" is because you made hundreds of thousands of dollars in index growth off limits, rather than selling some to boost the other two layers over the years.

Never selling feels safe—until the dividend gets cut.

The cc fund is not going to lose value like that.  I mean, if you want to buy a YieldMax fund, it will fall apart as advertised in probably only two years even during a bull market.  A well-constructed cc fund, however - from NEOS or Goldman Sachs - is not going to lose asset value in a bull or sideways market.  It probably will during a bear.  Time has yet to show how those funds will recover.  But this channel started off strong.  Now its pushing unsupported arguments to try to sell something.   oh well...

Trading after retirement can be a great way to explore new financial opportunities and potentially grow your wealth when approached with proper knowledge and risk management. After retiring, I decided to put my 401(k) funds to work through trading, and over time, I was able to make $600K, which gave me a new perspective on financial planning, investment opportunities, and the importance of making informed decisions about my retirement savings.

That’s some impressive growth. I’ve been working on improving my investment strategy, but I’m still looking for better ways to diversify my portfolio. I’m hoping to retire within the next few years, so I really want to make smarter moves with my investments.
